sources.headline: Why is Morocco celebrating the defeat of a UN resolution on Western Sahara?
sources.text: Morocco has welcomed the defeat of a US-drafted resolution which sought to extend the mandate of the UN mission in the disputed Western Sahara.The mandate of the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) expired on Saturday after a veto by Russia, leaving the future of the peacekeeping mission in limbo. In 1991, the UN established MINURSO to monitor a ceasefire and prepare a referendum on the territory’s future.Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Why does Spain have ‘enclaves’ in North Africa?list 2 of 3Morocco rejects accusations it was involved in Ceuta migrant influxlist 3 of 3Why Spain’s new Sahrawi citizenship law matters to Moroccoend of listMorocco has considered Western Sahara its own territory since 1975, when Spain withdrew from the desert region in northwest Africa which is roughly the size of Britain. The Algeria-backed Polisario Front seeks to establish an independent state called the Sahrawi Republic.So, why is Morocco celebrating the failed UN resolution? What does it mean for the future of the disputed region?Here is what we know:What happened at the UN Security Council?On Friday, the US, which is a permanent member of the UN Security Council, proposed a resolution to support the principle of self-determination in the disputed Western Sahara.Russia vetoed the resolution, despite support from 11 of the 15 council members, including fellow permanent members France and the United Kingdom.The US draft would have extended the mission for a year, removed “referendum” from its name and made Morocco’s autonomy proposal the only basis for further talks.Last October, the UN Security Council adopted a resolution that offered genuine autonomy to Western Sahara. Under that plan, the territory would manage its internal affairs, but remain under Moroccan sovereignty.The Security Council had already made the proposal a basis for negotiations last year and asked UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres to submit a review of the peacekeeping mission.Speaking after the vote, US ambassador Mike Waltz said it was truly unfortunate that in 2026 the veto was used to “preserve the letter R (in the Mission’s name) for referendum”.He added that Washington’s proposal “would have moved the 50-year conflict forward” and added that the status quo is not acceptable.Russia’s UN ambassador, Vassily Nebenzia, said at the same meeting that Moscow opposed the draft because it favoured one side.“We stress the fact that the Security Council cannot automatically predetermine matters relating to sovereignty,” he said.Instead, Russia proposed renewing the existing mission without those changes. But that draft also failed to secure the nine votes needed for adoption, receiving two votes in favour, one against and 11 abstentions.MINURSO’s mission has 155 military personnel and is set to cost $62m in the fiscal year that began in June, according to a UN report. But its mandate expired on Saturday.How did Morocco and Algeria react to the failure of the UN mission?Morocco’s royal palace welcomed the failure to renew MINURSO, saying on Friday that UN personnel and equipment should leave the territory in the coming days and that the Western Sahara issue should now be withdrawn from the Security Council’s consideration. Morocco said it remained committed to the ceasefire.According to a UN media statement, Morocco’s UN representative also questioned why Algeria’s delegate was giving the Security Council “lectures” on the Western Sahara.“Let these people [in the Western Sahara] go back to Morocco,” he said, “let them go home”.Algeria expressed regret on Saturday over the failure to renew MINURSO’s mandate. Its foreign ministry criticised what it described as the US draft’s excessive bias towards Morocco.According to a UN media statement, Algeria’s delegate to the UN thanked Russia for its draft resolution and all other member nations “who have chosen not to associate themselves” with an egregious injustice and a flagrant attack on “the very foundation of our organisation”.Algeria’s UN representative noted that the country has been a refuge for hundreds of thousands of Sahrawi people who have been denied their right to self-determination.The “tragedy being endured by the Sahrawi people has oddly been diluted to the concept of refugee populations”, he added.Sidi Omar, the Polisario Front’s representative at the UN, told reporters on Friday that he welcomed Russia’s veto because the US proposal would undermine Sahrawi self-determination.What is the Western Sahara dispute all about?The Polisario Front, the political and military representative, does not recognise Morocco’s annexation of the territory following Spain’s withdrawal in 1975. It has been seeking a UN-supervised referendum for self-determination.In 1976, it declared the independent Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic.Decades of fighting drove at least 170,000 Indigenous people into refugee camps in Tindouf in neighbouring Algeria, which backs the Polisario Front.The Polisario Front signed a UN-brokered ceasefire with Morocco in 1991. It called for a referendum within six months, but it was never held.Morocco, which retains control of its lucrative phosphate and fishing resources in Western Sahara, claims historic and pre-colonial ties to the land and views the region as an integral part of its territory [“Greater Morocco”].For decades, the US has provided military and diplomatic support to Morocco. But in 2020, Donald Trump recognised Moroccan sovereignty over the territory during his first term in office. Morocco soon established diplomatic ties with Israel as part of the so-called Abraham Accords.The region is now the last United Nations-designated “non-self-governing territory” in Africa, where between 100,000 and 140,000 Moroccan military personnel are based.Low-level fighting has also continued since the Polisario Front said it was resuming armed struggle in 2020.Why is Morocco celebrating the failed UN resolution?MINURSO was set up to monitor the 1991 ceasefire and hold a referendum in Western Sahara. The expiry of its mandate will likely boost Morocco’s stance on the referendum question, though its autonomy proposal has already been adopted by the UN.On Saturday, according to a video report by the Reuters news agency, a festive atmosphere prevailed in the streets of El Aaiun, the capital of Western Sahara.In the central Mechoua Square, dozens of people were wearing melfas, the traditional Sahrawi women’s garments, and long robes known as darra, as they waved Moroccan flags and displayed portraits of Morocco’s King Mohammed VI.Selim Balouati Lakhloufi, a historian and researcher based in Morocco, said that Morocco is pleased because “diplomatic developments at the United Nations are supporting its strategy regarding the [disputed Western] Sahara”.“The support of powers such as the United States, France and the United Kingdom for Morocco’s autonomy proposal strengthens its international position and is gradually shifting the debate away from the right to self-determination and the possibility of independence toward a solution based on autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty,” he told Al Jazeera.What does this mean for the future of the Western Sahara?The collapse of MINURSO’s mandate could escalate the dispute in the Western Sahara, according to aid organisations.Oxfam has warned that losing MINURSO’s “monitoring and de-escalation functions risks undermining security and stability”.Lakhloufi said that the UN mission’s expiry is also unfavourable for Sahrawi independence aspirations.Regarding the future of the Western Sahara, he said that Morocco will likely continue to consolidate its territorial, economic and administrative control, while the Polisario Front will face greater difficulties in securing international support.“The proposal for autonomy could end up becoming the main framework for negotiations, pushing independence further and further out of reach,” he added.

UN’s peacekeeping mission in disputed Western Sahara ends after 35 years

The 35-year-old UN peacekeeping mission ⁠in the disputed Western ​Sahara region came to an end Sunday after the Security Council failed to ​renew its mandate. Morocco, which claims the region as its own, welcomed the decision, while its opponents from the Algeria-backed Polisario Front called it "unacceptable".

Issued on: 01/11/2026 - 21:37
Modified: 01/11/2026 - 21:43

  4 min
Reading time
Share
By:
FRANCE 24
The Guerguerat border post in Western Sahara. © Mohamed Siali, EFE

The UN's long-running peacekeeping mission for the disputed Western Sahara ceased operations Sunday after 35 years, as a result of a US-Russia standoff at UN headquarters over the territory’s future.

The end of the mission raises concerns about stability in the region. Rich in minerals and fisheries, Western Sahara is a vast desert territory roughly the size of Colorado along Africa’s northwestern Atlantic coast. Once ruled by Spain, it is claimed by both Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front.

“This 1 November 2026 marks the start of the liquidation period,” Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson for the UN secretary general, said in a statement. “A smaller team reporting to the United Nations’ Department of Operational Support will oversee the orderly transportation of assets belonging to troop-contributing countries to their respective nations, and the appropriate disposal of equipment belonging to the United Nations.''

The mission had been repeatedly extended since it was established in 1991. In the UN Security Council on Friday, Russia vetoed a draft US resolution that would have supported Morocco’s demand for sovereignty over Western Sahara and ended the peacekeeping mission next year.

Read moreGoogle denies removing Maps border between Western Sahara and Morocco

Then a rival Russian resolution to extend the mission was voted down. The disagreement led to an abrupt end of the force’s mandate.

Morocco’s royal palace welcomed the non-renewal of the mission. It called it an "instrument to internationalize the dispute".

The Polisario Front, backed by Algeria, called it "an unacceptable decision". The Algerian foreign ministry said it profoundly regrets the non-renewal of the mandate and criticized what it called the "excessive bias'' of the US draft resolution.

The UN classifies Western Sahara as a “non-self-governing territory”, while critics of Morocco’s control describe it as Africa’s last colony. Morocco administers nearly all of the disputed territory, except for a narrow strip known as the “free zone” that lies east of a Moroccan-built sand wall.

After Morocco annexed it in 1975, the dispute escalated into an armed conflict that lasted more than 15 years and claimed more than 16,000 lives on both sides, according to the French Senate.

Watch moreWinds and waves: Tourism takes off in disputed Western Sahara

Bringing Western Sahara under its full sovereignty has been a central objective of Morocco’s foreign policy for decades. Rabat, which has secured the backing of a growing number of Western capitals, including Washington, Paris and London, refers to the territory as its southern provinces. The dispute has become a defining feature of Morocco’s diplomacy, with the kingdom often measuring its relations with other countries by their position on the issue.

The Polisario Front seeks independence for the territory, which it considers the homeland of the Indigenous Sahrawi people. Operating from refugee camps in the Algerian city of Tindouf, the movement aims to establish an independent Sahrawi Republic. Mainly backed by Algeria, Russia and South Africa, the Polisario has seen its international support dwindle in recent years.

A UN-brokered cease-fire took effect in 1991. The agreement also paved the way for the creation of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, known as MINURSO.

The settlement plan provided for a referendum on self-determination, with independence among the options. But the vote never materialized. Morocco wanted the voter list to include Sahrawis living in the territory it controls, while the Polisario objected, arguing that their inclusion would tilt the outcome toward integration with Morocco. The movement insisted on using Spain’s colonial census to determine voter eligibility.

Watch moreMass investment changes face of Dakhla, in Morocco-controlled Western Sahara

Twenty MINURSO personnel lost their lives in the mission. The UN force was authorized to have 534 personnel, and its 2026-2027 budget was more than $62 million. The top military contributors to the force were Egypt, Ghana and Pakistan.

As the mission ends, the UN secretary-general "calls upon all parties to respect and promote the rights of the people of Western Sahara," Dujarric said, and "remains concerned about the security situation throughout the Territory and the risk of escalation of hostilities. He calls on all concerned to exercise maximum restraint."

The Polisario withdrew from the ceasefire in 2020 after clashes and the territory has since remained the scene of tensions and low-intensity hostilities, the UN said last month.

Western Sahara is the major flashpoint in the rivalry between regional heavyweights Morocco and Algeria. Algiers, which arms, funds and hosts the Polisario Front, sees full Moroccan sovereignty over the territory as a major diplomatic defeat. The two countries severed diplomatic relations in 2021, and the end of the mission risks further straining ties and fueling an arms race.

(FRANCE 24 with AP)

sources.headline: UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara ends after 35 years, UN chief says
sources.text: The 35-year-old UN peacekeeping mission in the Western Sahara region will come to an end after the Security Council failed to renew its mandate, the UN chief said on Nov 1.Morocco, which claims the Western Sahara as its own, welcomed the decision, while its opponents in the Algeria-backed Polisario Front expressed concern.The Polisario Front has been seeking an independent state in Western Sahara since former colonial power Spain left in 1976.A peacekeeping mission, known as MINURSO, has been in place there since a UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991.November 1 would mark the start of the “liquidation phase” of the mission, with assets transported back to troop-contributing countries, UN chief Antonio Guterres said in a statement.The end of the peacekeeping mission comes a year after the UN Security Council adopted a US-drafted resolution that accepted Rabat’s plan to give the territory autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty as the “most feasible” solution to the conflict.Russia, which abstained in last year’s vote, this year vetoed another US-backed resolution that would have cemented the UN’s preference for the Moroccan plan while scaling back the peacekeeping force.The Security Council then defeated a competing Russian resolution, leaving the mission to expire without a new mandate.Besides monitoring the ceasefire, MINURSO was tasked with organising a referendum that has never taken place due to disagreements over voter eligibility.Morocco’s Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita told state media that the mission’s reference to a referendum - the “R” in its name - was an “anachronism”.Rabat had been informed that Russia was going to block the US-drafted resolution, but saw it as “an opportunity to review certain rules of the game”, he said.Morocco’s royal palace had said the non-renewal of the mission was a “significant development” towards withdrawing the Western Sahara issue from consideration by the Security Council.Algeria’s Foreign Ministry on Oct 31 expressed “deep regret” over the non-renewal, blaming the “excessive bias” of the US towards Morocco’s position.The Polisario said in a statement it was “concerned at the deadlock in the Security Council meeting”. REUTERS
